0.title: Hope at the Last Enemy
0.overview:
Death is the one certainty of human life. Our culture does its best to avoid thinking about it. People die in hospitals rather than at home, funerals are short, and conversation about death is often considered morbid. Yet everyone will face it, both the death of those they love and their own.

Scripture does not avoid death. It speaks about it honestly and often. Death is an enemy, the wages of sin, a terrible intrusion into God's good world. And yet for those in Christ, death has lost its sting. Jesus said, I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live (John 11:25). The Christian faces death not with denial or despair but with sober realism and living hope.

This study is pastoral. It is not mainly about the debates over the order of end-time events, which the End Times Models study covers. It asks practical and personal questions. Why do we die? How did Christ conquer death? How can we prepare to die well? How should Christians grieve? What happens when we die? And what is heaven really like?

Six units: (1) The Last Enemy; (2) Christ Has Conquered Death; (3) Preparing to Die Well; (4) Grieving with Hope; (5) What Happens When We Die?; (6) The New Heavens and the New Earth.

1.title: The Last Enemy
1.overview:
Death was not part of the original creation. God made a world that was very good (Gen 1:31). He warned Adam that in the day he ate of the forbidden tree, you shall surely die (Gen 2:17). When Adam sinned, death came: for you are dust, and to dust you shall return (Gen 3:19). Death is not natural in the sense of being what God intended. It is an intruder.

Death is the result of sin. Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned (Rom 5:12). This does not mean that every individual death is a punishment for a particular sin. Babies die, and righteous people die young. But death as such is the consequence of humanity's rebellion against God. The wages of sin is death (Rom 6:23).

Death is an enemy. Paul calls it the last enemy to be destroyed (1 Cor 15:26). Christians should not pretend that death is beautiful or simply a natural part of life. When Jesus stood at the tomb of his friend Lazarus, he wept and was deeply moved (John 11:33-35). He was grieved and angry at death's destruction, even though he was about to raise Lazarus.

Death is certain. It is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment (Heb 9:27). Life is short: The years of our life are seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty; yet their span is but toil and trouble; they are soon gone, and we fly away (Ps 90:10). We do not know when our death will come.

Thinking about death is wise. It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting, for this is the end of all mankind, and the living will lay it to heart (Eccl 7:2). Funerals remind us of what really matters. Moses prayed, So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom (Ps 90:12). Remembering our mortality makes us humble, focused and ready.
1.theology:
Physical and spiritual death: Scripture speaks of death in more than one sense. Spiritual death is separation from God, the state of all people by nature (Eph 2:1). Physical death is the separation of soul from body. Eternal death, the second death, is final separation from God's favour (Rev 20:14). Christ saves from all three.

The fear of death: Hebrews speaks of those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery (Heb 2:15). Much human anxiety, ambition and distraction is driven by a hidden fear of death. Facing death honestly in the light of the gospel brings freedom.

Old age: Ecclesiastes 12 describes the decline of old age in vivid poetry: failing eyes, trembling hands, loss of strength. Scripture does not glamourise ageing. But it honours the old (Lev 19:32) and promises God's care to the end: even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you (Isa 46:4).
1.examples:
Then: In Genesis 5, the genealogy from Adam to Noah repeats a sombre refrain: and he died. Name after name, the same ending. But one man breaks the pattern: Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him (Gen 5:24). Even in the shadow of death, God gave a hint that death would not have the last word.

Now: A busy professional has never thought seriously about death. Then a colleague her own age dies suddenly. At the funeral, she realises how fragile life is. She begins to read the Bible again, asking what really lasts. The house of mourning taught her what the house of feasting never did.

A simple test: If you knew you would die this year, what would you change about how you are living?

verseByVerse.quote: And to Adam he said, "Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and have eaten of the tree of which I commanded you, 'You shall not eat of it,' cursed is the ground because of you; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life; thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you; and you shall eat the plants of the field. By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, till you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God's judgment on Adam touches his work and his life. The ground is cursed, work becomes toil, and life ends in death: dust returning to dust. Every funeral echoes these words. But the curse is not the end of the story. In the same chapter God promised the offspring of the woman who would crush the serpent (Gen 3:15).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned— for sin indeed was in the world before the law was given, but sin is not counted where there is no law. Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those whose sinning was not like the transgression of Adam, who was a type of the one who was to come. But the free gift is not like the trespass. For if many died through one man's trespass, much more have the grace of God and the free gift by the grace of that one man Jesus Christ abounded for many. And the free gift is not like the result of that one man's sin. For the judgment following one trespass brought condemnation, but the free gift following many trespasses brought justification. For if, because of one man's trespass, death reigned through that one man, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man Jesus Christ. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul traces death to Adam's sin. Through one man, sin and death spread to all. But then he contrasts Adam with Christ. If death reigned through one man's trespass, much more will those who receive grace reign in life through one man, Jesus Christ. Death came through a man; life comes through a man.

verseByVerse.quote: The years of our life are seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty; yet their span is but toil and trouble; they are soon gone, and we fly away. Who considers the power of your anger, and your wrath according to the fear of you? So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses reflects on the shortness of life and the reality of God's wrath against sin. Life is toil and trouble, and it passes quickly. The right response is not denial but prayer: teach us to number our days. Counting our days is not morbid; it is the beginning of wisdom.

verseByVerse.quote: A good name is better than precious ointment, and the day of death than the day of birth. It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting, for this is the end of all mankind, and the living will lay it to heart. Sorrow is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad. The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Preacher says the day of death is better than the day of birth, and the house of mourning better than the house of feasting. This sounds strange, but his point is that sorrow can make the heart wise. Facing death teaches us what life is for. Fools avoid the subject; the wise lay it to heart.

1.reflection:
Why is it important to see death as an enemy rather than a natural part of life?

Read Psalm 90. What does it mean to "number our days"?

How does our culture avoid thinking about death? How do you?

What has a funeral or the death of someone close to you taught you?

2.title: Christ Has Conquered Death
2.overview:
The heart of the Christian hope is not that death is unreal, but that Christ has defeated it.

He died our death. Jesus took on flesh and blood that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery (Heb 2:14-15). He entered death itself, bearing the penalty for sin. Because he has paid for sin, death no longer has a legal claim on those who belong to him.

He rose from the dead. On the third day, Jesus walked out of the tomb. He was not resuscitated to die again. He was raised to immortal, glorified life. We know that Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again; death no longer has dominion over him (Rom 6:9). His resurrection is the first-fruits of the harvest to come.

He holds the keys. The risen Christ said to John, Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades (Rev 1:17-18). Death is not in charge. Christ is. No believer will pass through the door of death except when he opens it, and he will be on the other side.

Death has lost its sting. O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting? The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Cor 15:55-57). For the believer, death is like a bee that has lost its sting. It can still frighten and hurt, but it cannot destroy. Its poison was drained into Christ.

Death is now a doorway. For Christians, death is no longer the end but a passage into the presence of Christ. Paul could say, For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain (Phil 1:21). Jesus spoke of the death of believers as sleep (John 11:11), not because they become unconscious, but because they will wake again.
2.theology:
The resurrection of the body: The Christian hope is not only that the soul goes to heaven, but that the body will be raised. Christ's resurrection is the pattern: the same body, transformed and glorified. God will not abandon the bodies he made.

Union with Christ in death: Believers die in Christ, and their bodies, even in the grave, remain united to him. They are the dead in Christ (1 Thess 4:16). Death cannot separate us from his love (Rom 8:38-39).

Christ abolished death: Paul says that Christ Jesus abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel (2 Tim 1:10). Death's final abolition awaits his return, but its defeat is already accomplished.
2.examples:
Then: At the tomb of Lazarus, Martha said she believed her brother would rise on the last day. Jesus said, I am the resurrection and the life. Then he called, Lazarus, come out, and the dead man came out (John 11:24-25, 43-44). The resurrection is not only a doctrine. It is a person, and he has power over the grave.

Now: An elderly Christian man, told by his doctor that he has weeks to live, is surprisingly calm. His grandson asks if he is afraid. He answers, "I'm not looking forward to the dying. But I'm not afraid of death. Jesus has been through it ahead of me, and he's waiting on the other side."

A simple test: Do you fear death? Bring that fear to the risen Christ, who holds the keys.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Your brother will rise again." Martha said to him, "I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day." Jesus said to her, "I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?" She said to him, "Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Martha believed in a future resurrection, but Jesus pointed her to himself. He is the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in him will live even though he dies, and whoever lives and believes in him will never die. Then he asks her, and us, Do you believe this? Everything depends on the answer.

verseByVerse.quote: Since therefore the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same things, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Son became human so that he could die. By his death he destroyed the devil's power over death and delivered those enslaved by the fear of death. Christians do not have to live in that fear any longer. The one who has the keys of death is our Saviour.

verseByVerse.quote: When the perishable puts on the imperishable, and the mortal puts on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written: "Death is swallowed up in victory." "O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?" The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul taunts death: where is your victory, where is your sting? The sting of death is sin, but Christ has dealt with sin. Then comes a practical conclusion: be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, because your labour in the Lord is not in vain. The resurrection gives eternal meaning to ordinary faithfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: When I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead. But he laid his right hand on me, saying, "Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: John fell at the feet of the glorified Christ as though dead. Jesus laid his hand on him and said, Fear not. He is the first and the last, the living one who died and is alive forevermore. And he holds the keys of Death and Hades. The believer's death is under Christ's control.

2.reflection:
How does Christ's death free us from the fear of death?

What does it mean that death has "lost its sting" for believers?

Read John 11:17-44. What does this story show about Jesus and death?

How does 1 Corinthians 15:58 connect the resurrection to everyday life?

3.title: Preparing to Die Well
3.overview:
In earlier centuries, Christians wrote books on "the art of dying well." They believed that preparation for death was part of a faithful life. Today, many people never think about death until it is upon them. Scripture encourages us to be ready.

Be ready spiritually. The most important preparation is to be right with God through faith in Christ. Jesus told of a rich man who planned to build bigger barns, but God said, Fool! This night your soul is required of you (Luke 12:20). Being rich toward God matters more than any earthly security. No one should put off repentance and faith, assuming they will have time later.

Be ready relationally. Death often reveals unfinished business: unforgiven wrongs, words left unsaid, broken relationships. While there is time, seek reconciliation, ask forgiveness, express love and gratitude, and bless those you leave behind.

Be ready practically. Caring for one's family includes practical preparation: making a will, arranging finances, discussing medical wishes and funeral plans. These are acts of love that spare grieving families confusion and conflict. But if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith (1 Tim 5:8).

Finish well. Paul, facing execution, wrote, I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith (2 Tim 4:7). He did not look back on a perfect life, but on a faithful one. He looked forward to the crown of righteousness (2 Tim 4:8). The goal is not merely to live long but to finish faithfully.

Die in hope. Paul's attitude was striking: My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better (Phil 1:23). Yet he was willing to remain for the sake of others. A Christian can hold both: a desire to be with Christ and a willingness to keep serving as long as God wills.
3.theology:
End-of-life decisions: Life is God's gift, and deliberately ending it is forbidden (Exod 20:13). This rules out euthanasia and assisted suicide, even when motivated by compassion. But Christians are not required to accept every possible treatment. It is right to decline treatments that are burdensome and offer little hope, and to accept good pain relief, even if it may shorten life as a side effect. The line is between allowing death and causing it.

Suicide: Taking one's own life is a grave sin. But it is not the unforgivable sin. A true believer who dies this way, in despair or illness of mind, is not cut off from the grace that saves sinners, for salvation rests on Christ's work, not on the state of our last moment (Rom 8:38-39). Anyone thinking of it should speak to someone today: a pastor, a friend, a doctor.

Deathbed conversions: The thief on the cross shows that it is never too late to turn to Christ (Luke 23:42-43). But it is dangerous to presume on it. Many die suddenly, and hearts harden over time.
3.examples:
Then: Before his death, Jacob gathered his sons and blessed each of them (Gen 49). Joseph, at the end of his life, made his brothers promise to carry his bones to the promised land (Gen 50:24-25). These men died looking forward to God's promises. These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar (Heb 11:13).

Now: A Christian woman diagnosed with a terminal illness uses her remaining months well. She makes a will, discusses her funeral with her pastor, choosing hymns of hope. She writes letters to her children and grandchildren, telling them how much she loves them and urging them to trust Christ. She reconciles with an estranged sister. When she dies, her family grieves deeply, but they have been given a gift.

A simple test: If you died tomorrow, what would you leave undone? What can you do about it this week?

verseByVerse.quote: And he told them a parable, saying, "The land of a rich man produced plentifully, and he thought to himself, 'What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops?' And he said, 'I will do this: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods. And I will say to my soul, "Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry."' But God said to him, 'Fool! This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?' So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The rich man's problem was not that he was wealthy, but that he planned his life as if death would never come. He spoke only to himself and thought only of ease. God called him a fool. The lesson: So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.

verseByVerse.quote: For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain. If I am to live in the flesh, that means fruitful labor for me. Yet which I shall choose I cannot tell. I am hard pressed between the two. My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better. But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account. Convinced of this, I know that I will remain and continue with you all, for your progress and joy in the faith, so that in me you may have ample cause to glory in Christ Jesus, because of my coming to you again. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul writes from prison, not knowing whether he will live or die. For him, to live is Christ and to die is gain. He longs to be with Christ, which is far better. But he also sees that remaining is necessary for the church. He holds both together in peace. This is the Christian attitude to death: longing, but not impatience.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am already being poured out as a drink offering, and the time of my departure has come. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award to me on that day, and not only to me but also to all who have loved his appearing. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: These are among Paul's last recorded words. He describes his death as a drink offering being poured out and as a departure. He has fought, finished and kept the faith. And he looks forward to the crown of righteousness, not only for himself but for all who have loved Christ's appearing. Paul died well because he had lived well.

verseByVerse.quote: These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar, and having acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth. For people who speak thus make it clear that they are seeking a homeland. If they had been thinking of that land from which they had gone out, they would have had opportunity to return. But as it is, they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The patriarchs died without receiving what God had promised. But they saw it from afar and welcomed it. They knew they were strangers and exiles on earth, seeking a better country. And God was not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city.

3.reflection:
What does it mean to be "rich toward God" (Luke 12:21)?

What practical preparations for death have you made? What remains to be done?

Is there a relationship you need to put right while there is time?

Read 2 Timothy 4:6-8. What would it mean for you to finish well?

4.title: Grieving with Hope
4.overview:
Christians grieve. Abraham wept for Sarah (Gen 23:2). David wept for Absalom (2 Sam 18:33). Jesus wept for Lazarus (John 11:35). Devout men made great lamentation over Stephen (Acts 8:2). Faith does not remove grief. Pretending to feel no sorrow is not spiritual maturity.

But not as those without hope. But we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thess 4:13). Paul does not say "do not grieve." He says grieve differently. Christian grief is real, sometimes deep and long. But it is grief with a horizon. We will see our loved ones in Christ again.

God is near. The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit (Ps 34:18). Grieving people often feel that God is far away. Scripture assures them he is closest when they are most broken. The Psalms of lament give words to grief: anger, confusion, exhaustion and longing.

Grief takes time. There is no timetable for grief. Waves of sorrow may return on anniversaries, at holidays, or unexpectedly at the sound of a song. This is normal. Grief is the cost of love.

Comforting the grieving. The church is called to weep with those who weep (Rom 12:15). Job's friends did best in the first week, when they sat with him in silence (Job 2:13). The most helpful comfort is often presence, not explanations. Practical help, such as meals, childcare and paperwork, is a gift. And remembering the bereaved months later, when others have moved on, is a great kindness.

When the dead were not believers. This is one of the hardest griefs. We cannot know what passed between a person and God in their final moments. We can leave them in the hands of the Judge of all the earth, who will do what is right (Gen 18:25), and trust that God's justice and mercy are perfect.
4.theology:
Infants who die: Do infants who die go to heaven? David expected to be with his son: I shall go to him, but he will not return to me (2 Sam 12:23). Scripture does not set out a full doctrine, and Christians have answered differently. But God is merciful, infants have not rejected him, and Jesus welcomed little children, for to such belongs the kingdom of heaven (Matt 19:14). Many in the Reformed tradition have held that God saves those who die in infancy, by his grace in Christ. Grieving parents may rest their little ones in God's hands with real hope.

Will we know each other? Scripture suggests we will. David expected to be with his son. Moses and Elijah were recognisable at the transfiguration (Matt 17:3). Paul expected to rejoice over the Thessalonians at Christ's coming (1 Thess 2:19). Relationships will be transformed, not erased.

Grief and complicated loss: Some grief is complicated by suicide, violence, estrangement or a difficult relationship. Such grief may need extra care and wise counsel. The Biblical Counseling study has a unit on grief and loss.
4.examples:
Then: When Lazarus died, Jesus came to Bethany. He knew he was about to raise him. Yet when he saw Mary and the others weeping, he was deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled, and he wept (John 11:33-35). The Lord who would conquer death still wept at its cruelty. He weeps with us.

Now: A widower in his sixties feels guilty for still grieving his wife a year after her death. People at church seem to expect him to have moved on. A friend reads him 1 Thessalonians 4:13 and says, "Paul doesn't tell you not to grieve. He tells you to grieve with hope. Take all the time you need." The widower weeps, and feels lighter.

A simple test: Who do you know who is grieving? How could you show them comfort this week?

verseByVerse.quote: But we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope. For since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep. For this we declare to you by a word from the Lord, that we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will not precede those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God. And the dead in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord. Therefore encourage one another with these words. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Thessalonians feared that believers who died before Christ's return had missed out. Paul assures them: the dead in Christ will rise first, and all believers will be together with the Lord. Grief is real, but it is not hopeless. Therefore encourage one another with these words.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet, saying to him, "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died." When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, he was deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled. And he said, "Where have you laid him?" They said to him, "Lord, come and see." Jesus wept. So the Jews said, "See how he loved him!" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Mary fell at Jesus' feet and said, Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. Jesus did not rebuke her honest grief. He was deeply moved, asked where Lazarus was laid and wept. The onlookers said, See how he loved him! Jesus' tears dignify ours.

verseByVerse.quote: When the righteous cry for help, the LORD hears and delivers them out of all their troubles. The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Lord hears the cry of the righteous. He is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit. This does not mean the righteous will escape affliction; the next verse says their afflictions are many (Ps 34:19). But the Lord delivers them out of them all, and he is near in the meantime.

verseByVerse.quote: But when David saw that his servants were whispering together, David understood that the child was dead. And David said to his servants, "Is the child dead?" They said, "He is dead." Then David arose from the earth and washed and anointed himself and changed his clothes. And he went into the house of the LORD and worshiped. He then went to his own house. And when he asked, they set food before him, and he ate. Then his servants said to him, "What is this thing that you have done? You fasted and wept for the child while he was alive; but when the child died, you arose and ate food." He said, "While the child was still alive, I fasted and wept, for I said, 'Who knows whether the LORD will be gracious to me, that the child may live?' But now he is dead. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he will not return to me." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: David had fasted and wept while his infant son was ill. When the child died, he rose, washed and worshipped. His servants were puzzled. David explained that he could not bring the child back, but I shall go to him. Grieving parents have taken comfort in these words for centuries.

4.reflection:
Why is it important that Jesus wept at Lazarus's tomb?

What does it mean to "grieve with hope"?

How can you comfort someone who is grieving without offering empty answers?

Read Psalm 34:17-22. How does it speak to grief?

5.title: What Happens When We Die?
5.overview:
What happens to a believer between death and the resurrection? Scripture does not tell us everything, but it tells us enough.

With Christ immediately. To the dying thief, Jesus said, Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43). Not someday, but today. Paul says that to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Cor 5:8). He longed to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better (Phil 1:23). For the believer, death is not a long sleep in nothingness but an immediate entrance into Christ's presence.

Conscious and at rest. The souls of believers are conscious after death. In Revelation, the souls of martyrs under the altar cry out to God and are given white robes (Rev 6:9-11). They are at rest from their labours (Rev 14:13). This is often called the intermediate state: a real, conscious, blessed existence with Christ while awaiting the resurrection of the body.

Not yet complete. The intermediate state is not the final goal. Believers who have died are with Christ, but they are still waiting for the resurrection of their bodies and the renewal of all things. The best is yet to come.

The unbelieving dead. Jesus' story of the rich man and Lazarus describes the rich man in torment after death, conscious and aware, with a great chasm fixed between him and Abraham's side (Luke 16:23-26). Death fixes a person's destiny. There is no second chance after death: it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment (Heb 9:27).

A soul without a body. In the intermediate state, the soul exists without the body. Paul describes this as being unclothed (2 Cor 5:4). He did not long for this state for its own sake. He longed to be further clothed, with the resurrection body. Our hope is not merely to escape the body but to receive it back, glorified.
5.theology:
The views. Some teach "soul sleep," that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection. The Roman Catholic Church teaches purgatory, a place of purifying suffering for many believers before they enter heaven. Others hold that believers go immediately and consciously into Christ's presence.

The verdict: Believers go immediately and consciously to be with Christ. Jesus' promise of "today" (Luke 23:43), Paul's "far better" (Phil 1:23) and the conscious souls in Revelation 6 rule out soul sleep. Purgatory has no basis in Scripture and contradicts the sufficiency of Christ's sacrifice: by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Heb 10:14). Nothing remains to be paid.

Praying for the dead: Since the destiny of the dead is fixed, Scripture gives no command or example of praying for the dead. We pray for the living and thank God for those who have died in faith.

Near-death experiences: Christians should be cautious about building beliefs on reported experiences of heaven or hell. Scripture, not experience, is our guide about what lies beyond death.
5.examples:
Then: As Stephen was being stoned, he saw the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at God's right hand. He prayed, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit (Acts 7:56, 59). He knew where he was going, and who would receive him.

Now: A young mother is terrified that when she dies she will simply cease to exist, or lie unconscious for centuries. Reading Luke 23:43 and Philippians 1:23, she finds great comfort. She will be with Christ, immediately and consciously. Her fear does not vanish overnight, but it loses its grip.

A simple test: When you think of a believing loved one who has died, do you picture them as gone, or as with Christ?

verseByVerse.quote: One of the criminals who were hanged railed at him, saying, "Are you not the Christ? Save yourself and us!" But the other rebuked him, saying, "Do you not fear God, since you are under the same sentence of condemnation? And we indeed justly, for we are receiving the due reward of our deeds; but this man has done nothing wrong." And he said, "Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom." And he said to him, "Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: One criminal mocked Jesus; the other rebuked him, admitted his own guilt and asked Jesus to remember him. Jesus promised more than he asked: today you will be with me in paradise. No baptism, no good works, no time to make amends. Just faith in the dying King, and the promise of paradise that very day.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know that if the tent that is our earthly home is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. For in this tent we groan, longing to put on our heavenly dwelling, if indeed by putting it on we may not be found naked. For while we are still in this tent, we groan, being burdened—not that we would be unclothed, but that we would be further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. He who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who has given us the Spirit as a guarantee. So we are always of good courage. We know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord, for we walk by faith, not by sight. Yes, we are of good courage, and we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul compares our body to a tent that will one day be taken down. Believers have a building from God, eternal in the heavens. We groan, longing for the resurrection body. In the meantime, to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord. Whether we live or die, we aim to please him.

verseByVerse.quote: For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain. If I am to live in the flesh, that means fruitful labor for me. Yet which I shall choose I cannot tell. I am hard pressed between the two. My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul weighs life and death. Life means fruitful labour. Death means being with Christ, which is far better. He is not weary of life or wishing to escape responsibility. He simply knows where he will be. For the believer, death is not a loss but a gain, because Christ is there.

verseByVerse.quote: When he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the witness they had borne. They cried out with a loud voice, "O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?" Then they were each given a white robe and told to rest a little longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers should be complete, who were to be killed as they themselves had been. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: John sees the souls of martyrs under the heavenly altar. They are conscious, they speak, and they ask God how long until he brings justice. They are given white robes and told to rest a little longer. The dead in Christ are alive, honoured and waiting, with us, for the final day.

5.reflection:
What does Jesus' word "today" (Luke 23:43) teach about what happens at death?

Why is the intermediate state "far better" but not yet the final goal?

How does Hebrews 10:14 answer the idea of purgatory?

How does it comfort you to know that believers who have died are with Christ now?

6.title: The New Heavens and the New Earth
6.overview:
Many Christians imagine heaven as an endless church service in the clouds, with disembodied souls floating on harps. The Bible's picture is far richer and more solid. The final hope is not that we leave the earth for heaven, but that heaven and earth are made new and joined forever.

A renewed creation. Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away (Rev 21:1). The creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption (Rom 8:21). God will not throw away his creation; he will renew it. Peter speaks of new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (2 Pet 3:13).

God with us. Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God (Rev 21:3). The goal of the whole Bible is fulfilled: God living with his people. And the centre of it all is the Lamb.

No more tears. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away (Rev 21:4). Every grief, disease, injustice and sin will be gone. Every wrong will be made right.

Resurrection bodies. Believers will live in real, physical bodies, raised imperishable, glorious and powerful (1 Cor 15:42-44). They will be like Christ's risen body (Phil 3:21). The disabled will run; the aged will be young; the broken will be whole.

What will we do? Scripture hints at a life full of meaning. We will worship God and see his face (Rev 22:3-4). We will reign with Christ (Rev 22:5). The glory and honour of the nations will be brought into the city (Rev 21:26). There will be feasting (Rev 19:9). It will not be boring. It will be life as it was always meant to be, without sin, forever.

Who will be there? Only those who belong to the Lamb. But nothing unclean will ever enter it... but only those who are written in the Lamb's book of life (Rev 21:27). The invitation is open now: let the one who is thirsty come (Rev 22:17).
6.theology:
Renewal, not replacement: Some think the present world will be completely destroyed and replaced. More likely, Scripture teaches a renewal through purifying judgment, as the flood purged but did not annihilate the world (2 Pet 3:6-7). There is continuity as well as transformation, just as Christ's resurrection body was the same body, glorified.

The amillennial hope: Isaiah's picture of new heavens and new earth, with long lives and the wolf and the lamb together (Isa 65:17-25), is best read as a description of the new creation in the language of the Old Testament world, rather than of a future earthly thousand-year reign. Christ will return once, raise the dead and usher in the eternal state.

Marriage in the new creation: Jesus said that in the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage (Matt 22:30). This is not a loss. Human marriage points to the marriage of Christ and his church, and in the new creation the reality will have come.
6.examples:
Then: John, exiled on the island of Patmos for his faith, was given a vision of the new Jerusalem coming down from heaven. In a world where Christians were persecuted and dying, he saw the end of the story: God wiping away every tear. That vision sustained the church through centuries of suffering.

Now: A young man with a severe disability has never walked. Reading 1 Corinthians 15 and Revelation 21, he realises that his body will be raised whole. He says to his pastor, "The first thing I'm going to do is run to Jesus." His hope is not escapism. It gives him strength for the hard days now.

A simple test: When you think of eternity, do you think of something vague and cloudy, or something solid and joyful? Read Revelation 21-22 and let Scripture shape your hope.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more. And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away." And he who was seated on the throne said, "Behold, I am making all things new." Also he said, "Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: John sees a new heaven and a new earth, the holy city coming down, and hears God's voice: God will dwell with his people. Every tear wiped away. No more death, mourning, crying or pain. And the one seated on the throne says, Behold, I am making all things new. This is the final chapter of the Bible's story, and it is the beginning of an endless one.

verseByVerse.quote: For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us. For the creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the sons of God. For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God. For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now. And not only the creation, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul compares present sufferings with future glory and says they are not worth comparing. Creation itself is groaning like a woman in labour, waiting to be set free. Believers also groan, waiting for the redemption of their bodies. The pain is real, but it is the pain of birth, not of death.

verseByVerse.quote: So is it with the resurrection of the dead. What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power. It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body. Thus it is written, "The first man Adam became a living being"; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. But it is not the spiritual that is first but the natural, and then the spiritual. The first man was from the earth, a man of dust; the second man is from heaven. As was the man of dust, so also are those who are of the dust, and as is the man of heaven, so also are those who are of heaven. Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul uses the image of a seed. What is sown perishable is raised imperishable; what is sown in dishonour is raised in glory; in weakness, raised in power; a natural body, raised a spiritual body, a body wholly governed by the Spirit. We have borne the image of Adam, and we shall bear the image of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb through the middle of the street of the city; also, on either side of the river, the tree of life with its twelve kinds of fruit, yielding its fruit each month. The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations. No longer will there be anything accursed, but the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him. They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. And night will be no more. They will need no light of lamp or sun, for the Lord God will be their light, and they will reign forever and ever. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The river of life flows from the throne. The tree of life, lost in Eden, is restored, and its leaves are for the healing of the nations. The curse is gone. God's servants worship him and see his face, and they reign forever. The Bible ends where it began, in a garden with God, but now the garden has become a city filled with the redeemed.

6.reflection:
How is the Bible's picture of the new creation different from popular ideas of heaven?

Which promise in Revelation 21:1-5 means most to you, and why?

What does Romans 8:18-23 teach about how we should view present suffering?

How should the hope of the new creation shape how you live today?
